bbc_card_1.headline: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
bbc_card_1.description: There is no certainty that the idea will ever get off the ground, let alone become a blueprint for other countries, writes Katya Adler.
bbc_card_1.article_content:
Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.

The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.

But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."

Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.

The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.

Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.

The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else.

"We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right.

Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.

This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians.

Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.

Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.

Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act".

But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in.

Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU.

But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs.

They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence.

Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too.

For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships.

But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership.

Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries.

No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example.

A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU.

Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc.

In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

bbc_card_2.headline: Why Canadians are ready for closer ties with Europe
bbc_card_2.description: People the BBC spoke to are excited by the prospect of working and studying in the EU, a suggestion Carney made this week.
bbc_card_2.article_content:
Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc.

"I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto.

Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy.

"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said.

Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".

But before Canadians start packing their bags - "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement.

Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread.

Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits.

"It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said.

Canadian social media has lit up with the topic.

One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France.

"Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter.

The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US.

Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool.

"I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower.

But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation.

"I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said.

Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US.

"It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe."

For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music.

"I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added.

"However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals."

These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city.

Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons.

Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations.

The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021.

A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America.

However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce.

A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards.

"It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday.

Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations.

And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble.

"I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil.

Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems."

But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil.

"I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid."

With additional reporting by Madeline Halpert and James FitzGerald

bbc_card_3.headline: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
bbc_card_3.description: Buckingham Palace has strongly pushed back against claims in a new book by the late Princess of Wales's brother.
bbc_card_3.article_content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.

In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news.

Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book, after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough."

A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light.

The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago.

What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes.

Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris.

In excerpts from Earl Spencer's memoir published in the Daily Mail, he recounts being alerted to the car crash on 31 August, 1997, by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa.

During the calls that followed, which confirmed the death, the then-Prince Charles telephoned him, he writes.

The book alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time."

According to Earl Spencer, Charles informed him he had told Princes William and Harry of their mother's death first thing that morning, in their bedrooms at Balmoral.

The royal couple had divorced in August 1996.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week. BBC News has not seen the book in full.

In the memoir, Earl Spencer writes of his sister's troubled marriage - claiming a friend of Diana's had told him that on the eve of their wedding in July 1981, Prince Charles had told her he was "very happy to marry her, but… not actually in love with her".

Things became "very difficult indeed" in the marriage early on, Earl Spencer writes, adding that he is "sure that both spouses despaired of the other at times".

He now believes his sister had attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and as part of her condition suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria - describing the latter as an "intense emotional pain in the face of others' rejection or criticism".

In her later years, he writes, Princess Diana considered taking her own life on more than one occasion but love for her sons "stopped her from going further".

bbc_card_4.headline: US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York as war passes half-year mark
bbc_card_4.description: The BBC understands Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are among the delegates allowed to enter the US.
bbc_card_4.article_content:
The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month.

The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products.

The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries.

"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC.

"The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."

Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars.

State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott said the US would prevent the diplomats from "going on shopping sprees" as the Iranian people deal with water and electricity shortages, "brutal repression", and "soaring inflation".

"We will not let the Iranian regime's elites exploit UNGA for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people's suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran's wealth to support its terrorist proxies," he posted on X, warning New York shops to "be on guard" against selling goods to the delegation.

He did not indicate if the US was aware of any specific plans from the delegation to buy luxury items.

The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday.

Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron.

Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran.

Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.

Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.

The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA.

The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

bbc_card_5.headline: This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
bbc_card_5.description: Queensland's Fitzroy River has been selected for the 2032 Games, despite concerns over the course - and its inhabitants.
bbc_card_5.article_content:
The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.

Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.

"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.

But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.

While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.

And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.

"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.

Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.

"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.

"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."

The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.

But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.

"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.

"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."

Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.

But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.

Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".

Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.

On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.

There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.

The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."

In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.

The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.

But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.

The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.

So what about the crocodiles?

They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.

The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.

"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.

"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."

Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".

Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.

The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.

"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.

Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".

The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water.

Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games.

"For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School.

"The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally."

bbc_card_7.headline: Wife of US scholar jailed in China asks Trump to raise arrest at Xi meeting
bbc_card_7.description: Sylvia Zin is among the family members of people imprisoned in China who are seeking Trump's help when he hosts the country's leader next week.
bbc_card_7.article_content:
The wife of a US scholar imprisoned in China on charges of spying and endangering national security has asked President Donald Trump to secure his release when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next week.

U Min Zin, the director at a think tank focused on Myanmar, was arrested on 3 June after travelling to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference.

"I'm deeply hopeful that President Trump will raise my husband's case with President Xi Jinping at the summit next week," his wife, Sylvia Zin, testified to Congress on Wednesday.

Xi is due to arrive for a state visit to Washington DC on Wednesday. It comes after Xi hosted Trump for a visit to Beijing in May.

Ahead of the meeting, families of prisoners being held in China have travelled to the US capital to advocate for their release.

Sylvia Zin appeared before the House Foreign Affairs Committee East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee on Wednesday for a hearing titled Lives, Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea's Repression.

In her remarks, Zin said she believed Trump would also be able to secure the release of Chen Youlin, a US seismologist who tracks nuclear tests that has been held in prison in China for two years.

"Knowing the president's historic record on bringing wrongfully detained Americans home has reassured me that he will also be able to secure the swift release of Min Zin and other wrongfully detained citizens," she said.

Congresswoman Young Kim, the chairwoman of the subcommittee, opened the hearing by warning Americans: "If you travel to China, Beijing may take you hostage as leverage in diplomatic negotiation."

Speaking about Zin's arrest, she added: "Beijing wanted to send a message to those whose research inconvenienced it, and detained Mr Zin ahead of the upcoming Trump-Xi summit."

Min Zin, a student activist during Myanmar's 1988 pro-democracy movement, directs the Myanmar Institute for Strategic and Policy Studies (ISP-Myanmar), a think tank that studies China's role in Myanmar, including Chinese interests, relations, and regional influence.

The son of Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai also appeared on Capitol Hill to call on Trump to secure his father's release. The US president previously raised the case with Xi, telling reporters that his Chinese counterpart "told me that would be a tough one".

Asked for comment on Thursday, a senior White House official, speaking anonymously, told the BBC: "Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the President."

Last month, the US State Department said that two Americans - U Min Zin and Chen Youlin - were being "wrongfully detained" in China.

This designation in the US allows the cases to be transferred to the office of the Special Envoy for Hostage Affairs - raising the profile of each case and allowing the US government to allocate more resources to securing their release.

Zin, who lives in Thailand, told the committee on Wednesday that she has not yet been able to speak to her husband in jail, "so every month, we anxiously await his consular visits because they reassure us that he is alive".

Zin said US officials had told her that Min Zin was being subjected to up to six hours of interrogations each day when he first arrived in jail.

"I'm trying to be strong for our daughter, but I'm constantly wondering if he's OK and how to get him back home to us," she said.

Last time Trump and Xi formally met, Trump pressed for the return of another American in jail. Underground church leader Jin Mingri was freed two months after Trump's request.

bbc_card_8.headline: White House withdraws Trump's ICE nominee as Republican senator objects
bbc_card_8.description: One senator from Trump's party blocked the bid as he demands information about the fatal killings of US citizens by immigration enforcement.
bbc_card_8.article_content:
The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump's nominee to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after a Republican senator joined Democrats in opposing his confirmation.

Richard Schroyer was serving as a senior aide to the secretary of Homeland Security when Trump picked him to lead the immigration enforcement agency in June.

The White House withdrew his nomination on Thursday in a short memo, which did not explain the decision. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Republican Sen Rand Paul had stalled the nomination as he pressed for more information about ICE and Border Patrol shootings that killed two Americans in Minneapolis in January.

Schroyer had worked with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol for 29 years, and also served in the US Marines. He is a close ally of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose department oversees ICE and other immigration and border agencies. His selection by Trump was seen as a surprise given his lack of experience overseeing such a large law enforcement agency.

The position is one of many that needs to be confirmed by the US Senate. Schroyer's nomination did not manage to make it to a full Senate vote and had stalled in the Senate's Homeland Security committee.

ICE has not been led by Senate-confirmed leader since 2017 and instead has had a host of temporary chiefs. It is currently led by David Venturella, a former private prison executive, after Todd Lyon announced his departure from the top job in April.

The withdrawal on Thursday marks a defeat for Trump and Mullin, as the White House continues Trump's campaign pledge to lead the largest deportation effort in US history.

Paul, who serves as chairman of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said he would not advance the nomination to a full vote until the White House provided more information about the Minneapolis killings.

National protests took place earlier this year following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.

Both US citizens, the two were protesting when they were fatally shot in separate confrontations with ICE agents in January.

One of the promises that helped Trump take the White House in 2024 - cracking down on illegal immigration - has now divided voters going into the congressional midterm elections less than two months from now.

At the same time, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican from Florida, is warning that the crackdown could cause many of the Hispanic voters who supported him to turn their backs on the party when they go to the polls in November.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," she said in an advertisement filmed outside the White House that was released on Thursday. "Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

card_1.headline: Germany news: Mysterious explosions reported in Frankfurt
card_1.description: A cafe and kiosk were damaged overnight in what police said are the latest in a series of mysterious blasts. Follow DW.
card_1.article_content:
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Thursday, September 17, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faces a crucial weekend as voters go to the polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

After his CDU’s heavy defeat in Saxony-Anhalt, could another poor showing further weaken his leadership?

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz held a phone call with US President Donald Trump, where the two discussed the 9/11 attacks, the war in Ukraine and the situation in the Middle East.

German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Merz highlighted the special bond between Germans and US nationals.

A key topic of the call was the next steps toward ending the war in Ukraine.

"Chancellor Merz praised the passage of the Graham sanctions act by Congress," Kornelius said.

The bill calls for greater US sanctions on Russia. It was approved Wednesday by the House of Representatives and earlier by the Senate after the death of its champion, the late Senator Lindsey Graham.

In relation to the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, both leaders agreed that both waterways needed to be reopened swiftly, Kornelius said.

Despite the friendly call,relations between Germany and the US remain strained, since Merz cirticized US policy in the war in Iran.

Addressing a campaign event in Berlin ahead of the city's election on Sunday, Merz said the era of "unconditional transatlantic friendship" is likely over for the foreseeable future.

He said Europe has witnessed a "shift in the political stance on the other side of the Atlantic."

"It was long overdue for us to take on more responsibility for ourselves," Merz said, referring to his government's increased defense spending.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran's Foreign Ministry summoned Germany's ambassador in the country to voice protest over what it called "inappropriate statements" by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Merz had demanded that Iran stop its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, cease its support for armed groups such as Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in the Palestinian territories, and end its "military nuclear program."

Iran denies developing nuclear weapons, saying its program is purely for civilian purposes.

Foreign Ministry director Alireza Yousefi "conveyed the Islamic Republic of Iran's strong protest" against Merz's comments, calling them "unjustified and destructive."

The German ambassador in Tehran was also summoned in June after Merz said that Israel "is doing the dirty work for all of us," referring tothe country's war with Iran.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider spoke at the inauguration ceremony in Hamburg for Germany's largest offshore wind park to date on Thursday.

Windpark He Dreiht off the Germany's northern Baltic coast incorporates 64 wind turbines, which can in theory provide roughly 1.1 million households with electricity.

Schneider called the opening of the facility good news for Germany as an industial producers. He said that renewable energies were not just the most environmentally friendly, but nowadays "also the cheapest and most secure way to generate electricity."

He said the construction was "economic common sense" given the billions Germany currently pays for fossil fuel imports.

"Therefore, the quicker we make ourselves independent and generate our power from our own local energy sources, the better," he said.

The offshore wind park lies around 85 kilometers northwest of Borkum and 110 kilometers west of Helgoland in the Baltic Sea. According to its owner, power company EnBW, the park should eventually account for almost 10% of Germany's offshore wind capacity in its own right.

EnBW said that it had not required any state subsidies to raised investments of around €2.4 billion (roughly $2.75 billion) for the project. The project will take some time to reach full capacity and output, as the individual turbines are being activiated and connected to the grid one by one.

"The first turbines are already providing electricity, more will progressively follow," EnBW said, saying that it currently hoped to complete the activation process in a matter of months.

Cologne police have issued a warning about a particular WhatsApp hacking tactic, saying they were issuing the alert "in light of recent events."

It said its criminal investigative unit, Kripo Köln, "is currently working on cases" involving what it called "ghost pairing."

Police said that criminals might first use a hacked WhatsApp account to pose as somebody's daughter, son, friend or acquaintance.

They would ask them to click on a link or scan a QR code and subsequently to confirm connecting a device. In what police said was a real-world example, scammers falsely claimed it was a vote for a friend's daughter that would give her a chance of winning free dance lessons.

"Someone who believes they are just taking part in a seemingly harmless vote is in fact linking their own WhatsApp account to the perpetrator's smartphone," police wrote. "This person can immediately not just read or delete any messages. They can also chat with contacts in the name of the unsuspecting victim — for instance asking them to transfer money. And all this, thile WhatsApp continues to operate entirely normally on the victim's phone. This is what makes the scam so hard to detect."

The solution, police said, was to be vigilant whenever asked to click on links or scan QR codes, even by known contacts — and even more so with requests to pair of link devices.

People who suspected they might have fallen prey could check easily in their own Whatsapp settings, by going to "Profile," then to "Linked devices" and unpairing any devices they did not recognize, police said.

The private broadcasters RTL and Sky in Germany plan to cut about 500 jobs as part of their merger.

The RTL group, which bought out Sky Deutschland this year, confirmed the plans after they were first reported in the Bild newspaper on Thursday.

It said that most of the downsizing and restructuring was already complete and had been carried out in close coordination with works councils and unions. It said many of the cuts were achieved by not renewing expiring contracts or not hiring to fill open positions, in a bid to minimize layoffs or redundancies.

It did not say how the losses were split between the two companies.

The German arm of the RTL Group — a Luxembourg-based company that broadcasts in a string of other European countries like Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands — acquired Sky Deutschland in a bid to strengthen its position in the streaming and sports markets in Germany.

It was already effectively competing with Sky in broadcasting sports like Formula 1 and football.

It said it hoped the takeover would create "synergies" worth some €250 million (roughly $290 million), albeit primarily thanks to "optimization of content and of material costs" rather than personnel savings.

"Beyond that, duplicate structures will be dismantled, responsibilities will be bundled, and more efficient and forward-looking decision-making processes will be established," RTL said when announcing the takeover.

According to company data, RTL Germany currently employs 5,326 people and Sky has 2,170 employees.

A 24-year-old Iraqi man has been arrested in Germany on suspicion of planning attacks on a church in the northern city of Bremen, among other targets, federal prosecutors have said.

The man was arrested in the Barnim region of Brandenburg state, just outside Germany's capital city, Berlin.

The man is believed to adhere to the radical, militant ideology promoted by the Islamic State (IS) terror group.

Prosecutors say the man allegedly procured a firearm and was scouting out the church in Bremen as the first of several potential targets.

The federal prosecutors, headquartered in the southwestern city of Karlsruhe, also say the man tried to recruit at least one other person for the plot. That person remains unknown, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (Bundeskriminalamt or BKA) said in a statement.

The suspect has been placed in pre-trial detention, accused of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state, trying to form a terrorist organization and violating the weapons act, the BKA said.

IS has claimed responsibility for some of the worst terror attacks in Germany's history, including the attack on the Berlin Christmas market in 2016 and a knife attack in the western city of Solingen in 2024.

A nurse in Bavaria is charged with sexually abusing disabled patients, including many young children, in his care over the course of several years.

Prosecutors in Bamberg said on Thursday that a 33-year-old man was in investigative detention, accused of abusing 24 different people in three institutions in the southern state since October 2018. Some were under the age of 14.

He's alleged to have taken photographs and videos of the victims and to have touched several of them inappropriately.

Investigators believe that "as a result of their severe physical and mental impairments, [the victims] were unable to recognize and understand the offenses committed against them as such."

The investgiation was launched after German investigators received a tip-off from the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) about several sexually explicit videos of children that had been uploaded to a cloud online.

On searching the man's flat earlier this year, investigators secured more than 38,000 child pornography images and more than 600 videos.

The nurse is accused of the production and possession of child pornography, the sexual abuse of children, patients and vulnerable individuals in his care, and infringement of privacy and personal rights by taking photos and recording people without their understanding or consent.

Bamberg's regional court must now decided if it believes the case should go to trial. The nurse could face a jail term of between 1 and 15 years.

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has called on the EU to expand tariffs on Chinese imports to include hybrid cars, saying Chinese manufacturing subsidies endanger Volkswagen and other companies.

KIingbeil made the call on a visit to VW's Wolfsburg HQ in Lower Saxony; it coincided with a joint appeal from the heads of Germany's three major carmaking states, Bavaria (BMW, Audi), Baden-Württemberg (Porsche, Mercedes) and Lower Saxony (VW).

"I am in favor of us standing up against unfair trade practices, and for Germany to adopt a different level of self-confidence and assertiveness towards countries that threaten our industry," Klingbeil, who leads the Social Democrats and is also deputy chancellor, said in Wolfsburg.

The VW Group is just embarking on a major restructuring and cost-cutting drive amid falling sales figures, planning to cut or otherwise phase out as may as 100,000 jobs in the coming years across its various marques — almost a sixth of its workforce.

The unpopular restructuring was approved earlier this month despite resistance from trade unions and from Lower Saxony's state government, which is led by Klingbeil's center-left Social Democrats (SPD). Klingbeil said it should be just the beginning of an ongoing transformation.

He said the EU would have to tighten local content rules and introduce tariffs on Chinese-made plug-in hybrid cars.

In what seemed a coordinated appeal, the state premiers of Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg and Lower Saxony, each representing a different German political party, appealed to the federal government in Berlin and authorities in Brussels to act with haste to protect the car industry.

"Without a combination of competitive conditions in the domestic market, effective protective instruments and fair trade within the bounds of the WTO, the car industry is threatened with irreversible damage," state premiers Markus Söder (Bavaria), Olaf Lies (Lower Saxony) and Cem Özdemir (Baden-Württemberg) wrote.

Söder belongs to the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), Lies is in the SPD and Özdemir belongs to the environmentalist Greens.

The three premiers called for tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrids, to be modeled on existing fees imposted on all-electric cars from China.

In 2025 alone, the German car industry shed more than 50,000 jobs.

A German court on Thursday ruled that Facebook parent company Meta is liable for fake advertising on its social media platforms.

The case involved ads using the logo of a financial advice website, alongside photos of the website's founder, to promote fraudulent investment schemes.

The Frankfurt regional court found that Meta was liable, citing a European Court of Justice (ECJ) decision ruling a service provider is liable for content that it exercises control over.

Meta was ordered to cease the publication and distribution of the fake ads, compensate the claimant for any damages, and disclose the revenue generated.

Meta had argued that it had no knowledge of the fake ads, but the Frankfurt court said it was up to the social media giant to decide how ads are published on its platforms.

The decision can be appealed, and a spokesperson for Meta said the company was considering further legal steps. Meta said it had taken several measures in the case, including removing the content after it was reported.

Extreme heat and drought over the summer will lead to a weak potato harvest in northwestern Europe for 2026, according to an analysis released on Thursday by the UK-based Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).

In Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands the 2026 harvest is expected to fall a combined 3.1 million tons short of the five-year average harvest

The data shows the weak harvest will hit Germany particularly hard, with the country's share of the total expected potato harvest shortage coming in at 1,13 million tons.

These figures do not yet represent a final harvest report, but are an estimate.

"As fall begins, the effects of the record-breaking summer heat and drought on food and agriculture are becoming clear," said ECIU analyst Tom Lancaster.

Potatoes are among the crops in Europe that require the most water.

The analysis also reports a significant increase in prices. In Germany, spuds served at dinner are set to cost up to €280 per metric ton, compared to around €150 last year.

The expected 2026 harvest shortfall comes after oversupply in 2025 flooded the market.

No matter how you slice it, potatoes make up a large part of the average German diet. Whether in soups, mashed, fried, or served as French fries or chips, an average of roughly 60-65 kilograms of potatoes are eaten per person per year in Germany.

Native to the Bolivian and Peruvian Andes, the potato first arrived in Germany in 1630. According to legend, King Frederick II of Prussia believed in the economic and nutritious value of potatoes. He tricked local farmers into planting more of the so-called apple of the earth by posting soldiers around the potato fields to protect them. It worked — highly valued goods taste even better.

With over 5,000 varieties of potatoes now grown today, it's important to select the right fruit for your dish. Potatoes are sorted not by color, but by how they cook up. The firm and dense types are best for frying or making potato salad, while the fluffy, floury sorts are ideal for mashing and baking.

Pot lucks can prove problematic in Germany, since potato salad is a popular dish to bring. However, everyone's version is different. Some smother the sliced potatoes in hot oil and bacon; others prefer theirs chilled and coated in mayonnaise and accompanied by pickles. Either way, German potato salad is a must at any grill party.

Hearty German fare often includes potato dumplings, which come in different varieties. Some are made with cooked, mashed potatoes, while others mixed with flour for a starker consistency. Known as either Klösse or Knödel, the potato dumpling is a favorite side with pork roast.

Much of those 60-odd kilograms eaten by the average German each year must come from potato chips, considering it takes 10,000 kilograms of potatoes to make 2,500 kilograms of chips. Although chips are not native to Germany, some of the flavor choices are. Originally limited to only paprika or salt, flavors now include currywurst, ketchup and mayonnaise — and even the African sauce chakalaka.

Known as "Pommes" in Germany, French fries are often served with currywurst (pictured) or as a side dish with any other hearty meal. But street vendors also sell them all by themselves, often in paper cones and with a wooden fork - a trend in neighboring Holland and Belgium, too. They are offered with a wide variety of sauces, included standard ketchup, curry-flavored ketchup and mayonnaise.

A delicious, utterly basic dish that gets a lot of play in the German kitchen, potatoes are often served without being peeled. Served with a hefty helping of a herbed "Quark" (like yogurt) and a side salad, the "Pellkartoffel" will fill you up — even without a portion of meat.

"Reibekuchen" or "Kartofellpuffer" are shredded potatoes mixed with onions, deep fried and topped with applesauce, molasses or smoked salmon and yogurt sauce. They are a delicacy found at many Christmas markets in Germany. Popular with kids, the potato pancake can be quite filling despite its simplicity — but they're greasy, so grab a napkin when you buy them to-go.

It seems Germans don't just like to eat potatoes — they also like to talk about them, as potatoes play a central role in German idioms, too. While the "dumbest farmer harvests the fattest potatoes" is a lament in German, it's similar to the English "fortune favors fools." And being dropped like a hot potato can happen no matter your native tongue.

Karin Prien, Germany's education minister, backed plans to restrict social media use among young people and children. "Any system will have to comply with data protection rules and minimize the amount of information that is collected about the user, without age-verification data being transmitted online. However, the primary responsibility for protecting minors lies with the social media platforms themselves," Prien told German public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday.

In addition to requesting age checks, Prien said media education and providing more information on the issue for parents were key. On Wednesday, the president of the European Commission,Ursula von der Leyen, proposed that children under the age of 13 be banned from accessing social media platforms such asTikTok, Snapchat, and Instagram. They would be able to use "mini-accounts" controlled and supervised by parents, with a maximum usage of one hour per day, and open a separate account from the age of 15.

Prien said the restrictions should be part of a broader, more comprehensive strategy. She also called for a rule under which children under the age of three have no screen time or access to digital services. The education minister announced plans as early as October for a German interim solution while rules are consolidated at the EU level. Under the EU proposals, social media platforms would be required to introduce safer designs, including measures to prevent endless scrolling and videos from playing automatically. The plans also include limits on screen time and other measures aimed at protecting young people.

Kicking off his tenure as Germany's new head coach, Jürgen Klopp has named a huge squad of 44 players for his first four games, splitting them into two groups. A host of new faces is included.

Read the full story here.

Jürgen Klopp played professional football for 15 years, spending 11 of them in Mainz. He only reached the second division in Germany. beginning as an attacking player but ended his career as a defender. He retired midway through the 2001-02 season to fill the coaching vacancy at Mainz after the club sacked Eckhard Krautzun.

During Klopp's playing career, Mainz frequently fought against relegation to the German third tier. That changed when he took the helm at the club. In Klopp's third season, Mainz earned promotion to the Bundesliga for the first time in club history. Klopp enjoyed three seasons in the top flight before Mainz were relegated again in 2007. He left the club a year later to join Borussia Dortmund.

Klopp's appointment was part of a broader strategy change at Borussia Dortmund: to develop football stars instead of buying them. He committed to 20-year-olds Mats Hummels and Neven Subotic as his center back pair — the youngest in the Bundesliga. Dortmund finished in sixth place and fifth place in his first two seasons at the club.

From 2010 to 2012, Klopp led Dortmund to their most successful two-year stretch in club history. They won their first Bundesliga title in nearly a decade in 2010-11. Klopp followed that accomplishment up by leading BVB to their first domestic double in club history the next season.

It didn't take long for Dortmund fans to fall in love with Klopp. His press conferences became a weekly spectacle and his energy on the touchline became contagious. On the pitch, he implemented an active, high-pressing system that brought BVB, a club that was only a few years removed from near-insolvency, back to the pinnacle of German football.

Klopp did not secure domestic silverware after that two-year run, but he did lead Dortmund to the Champions League final in 2013 — their first final since their 1997 title. His side ultimately came up short against Bayern Munich, losing 2-1 late on to hand their German rivals a piece of their treble that year.

Klopp's last season with Dortmund in 2014-15 was far worse than any other. His side were second-to-bottom at the winter break, though Klopp wound up leading them to a seventh-place finish. He did manage to get BVB to the German Cup final before losing to Wolfsburg. Dortmund and Klopp decided to part ways after the season, ending his seven-year stint with the team.

It didn't take long for Klopp to land back on his feet. Liverpool appointed the German coach in October of 2015, less than five months after he parted ways with Dortmund. In his first press conference, Klopp dubbed himself "The Normal One" — after being asked how he fitted in compared to the likes of Jose Mourinho, who notoriously once called himself "a special one."

Liverpool fans took to Klopp's highly animated coaching approach, but it didn't initally lead to success. The Reds finished eighth in the Premier League in his first season, though he did lead them to the Europa League final before losing to Sevilla. But he guided Liverpool to the Champions League with a fourth-place finish the following season.

Much like he was in Dortmund, Klopp became a club favorite at Liverpool. His passionate personality and the attractive attacking football enabled by players like Mohamed Salah and Sadio Mane proved a real hit in the stands.

In 2018, Jürgen Klopp guided Liverpool to the brink of the biggest title in European club football. However, an injury to Mo Salah and two blunders by German goalkeeper Loris Karius put paid to Liverpool's hopes of winning the Champions League as Real Madrid made history at their expense.

A year later, Klopp got his revenge as Liverpool won the Champions League final against Tottenham. The European run was one for the ages, and included one of the greatest European comebacks of all time as Liverpool overturned a three-goal deficit against Barcelona to make the final. Liverpool lost the Premier League title by one point.

The following year, Klopp won the Premier League title with Liverpool. They also won the Club World Cup. In 2022, after a trophyless season, Klopp helped secure Liverpool a domestic double as they won both the FA Cup and League Cup. In January 2024, Klopp announced he was leaving, saying he had run out of energy. He left the club having won 8 major titles.

In a surprise to many, Klopp started a new role at Red Bull as "Global Head of Soccer" in January 2025. He was criticized for the move as the organization stood in opposition to much of what German football's traditions stand for and for having a multi-club model. In the role he provided strategic support to Red Bull clubs.

After Julian Nagelsmann's departure as Germany head coach has been named his successor – a job many believe he had long coveted. With Euro 2028 being hosted by the UK and Ireland, Klopp stands to get the chance to coach Germany in the familiar place where he had his greatest success to date as a coach.

Health authorities in Frankfurt are advising residents to consider taking precautions against mosquitoes after several recent malaria cases in the region believed to have been caused by the insects having stowed away on aircraft.

This week, two people living in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport were reported to have contracted malaria.

In August,  two Frankfurt Airport employees died after contracting malaria in an outbreak believed to have been caused by infected mosquitoes brought into Germany on an aircraft. Four other workers were infected, but recovered without complications.

The cases are part of a rare outbreak of so-called airport malaria, with the six employees infected despite not having traveled to a malaria-risk country. Authorities have not shared details about the two cases this week.

According to Germany's Robert Koch health institute, cases of airport malaria are extremely rare.

Data cited by DPA news agency shows that between 1969 and 2024, only 145 cases of locally contracted malaria were reported in Europe. At least 105 of those cases involved mosquitoes arriving on planes.

Most of these cases were in France, with only 9 reported in Germany in this time frame, making the 2026 outbreak a statistical outlier.

Malaria is native to tropical environments, and the vast majority of cases in Europe occur in summer.

card_3.headline: Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases
card_3.description: Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, more and more Russians are choosing to travel to Brazil to give birth.
card_3.article_content:
Yulia and Dmitri (whose names have been changed for reasons of safety) flew from Russia to Brazil this summer so that their child could be born there. Yulia was 32 weeks pregnant at the time of travel.

"Of course, we didn't say that I was pregnant at border control," Yulia told DW.

Her daughter was born at a private clinic in Santos, a city in southern Brazil. Anybody born in the country has an automatic right to Brazilian nationality. The family is currently preparing all the paperwork.

"We've achieved our minimum goal," said Dmitri. "With a Brazilian passport, our daughter will be able to travel without a visa to almost any country in the world. She won't have to apply for an expensive and time-consuming Schengen visa. We want her to be able to decide for herself where she studies, works or lives."

He said that a colleague of his had traveled to Brazil in early August with his pregnant wife for the same reasons.

Yulia and Dmitri said that they had spent the equivalent of about €10,000 (about $11,500) during the first six weeks of their stay in Brazil, which included the costs for several days of treatment for their daughter in intensive care. Dmitri quit his job at a bank for the trip and hopes to find work again after the family returns to their home in the Russian capital Moscow.

However, they are only planning to return once all the documents for their daughter are ready and that could take months. Other Russian families have decided to stay in Brazil permanently.

According to organizations and lawyers that provide support to Russians in Brazil, there has been an increase in immigration from Russia, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after which visa requirements for Russian nationals entering certain countries were tightened.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Birth tourism to Brazil has also increased since Argentina, which used to be one of the main destinations for people wanting their children to be born in a country that automatically grants citizenship to newborns, tightened its regulations. People who want their children to obtain Argentinian citizenship now have to have resided in Argentina for at least two years. Since 2025, the access of people who do not have a permanent residence permit to free healthcare has also been restricted.

According to the Russian news outlet RBC, more than 7,000 Russians applied for a residence permit in Argentina in 2023. By mid-2025, the number had decreased to about 1,800.

Meanwhile, almost 500 Brazilian passports were issued to Russians in 2024 and more than 600 the following year. More than half of the new citizens were women.

The parents of a child born in Brazil can apply for a residence permit, which they can obtain within a year, under certain circumstances.

Yana (name changed) and her husband chose to do this in 2023.

"The events of 2022 certainly played a role, but we had already toyed with the idea of giving birth abroad," Yana told DW. "A lot can happen in Russia. I always wanted a second passport and to give birth to my child in another country. When I became pregnant unexpectedly, all we had to do was decide which country made sense."

Yana gave birth to a boy at a public hospital in Florianopolis, the capital of the southern state of Santa Catarina, and the family stayed in Brazil for about three years.

"It was important to get passports for us and our child. I really enjoyed living there, and I learned Portuguese," Yana said, adding that she and her husband have lived as "digital nomads" in various countries over the years.

Even though they no longer live in Brazil, they want their son to have a connection to his birth country: "We read Portuguese books and talk a lot about Brazil. I want him to be able to travel without a visa and remain open to the world."

One of the largest Russian communities in Brazil lives in Florianopolis, and it's growing. According to the local health authorities, 119 Russian women took advantage of prenatal consultations in the first six months of this year. In all of 2025, it was 136 Russian women.

A lawyer who preferred to remain anonymous told DW that Brazil neither expressly prohibited nor permitted foreign nationals to enter the country for the purpose of giving birth. Often pregnant women do not disclose their reason for traveling to Brazil at border control. And once they are in the country they have access to free public hospitals and medical facilities regardless of their immigration status.

As Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases, a whole industry has emerged. Often, recent Russian immigrants to Brazil act as intermediaries and help others find housing or medical care. They provide assistance with complicated administrative procedures or the language. Depending on the level of care, the cost can reach into the thousands of dollars.

However, providers of such services, lawyers, and volunteers report stricter controls by Brazilian authorities, particularly in cities with larger Russian communities, such as Florianopolis. They say authorities are requesting more documents than in the past.

"The police are conducting more thorough checks to verify whether people actually live at the addresses they provide," one lawyer said, explaining that in the past, false addresses had been given by people hoping to obtain residence permits more quickly.

But DW did not find any evidence to suggest that Russians were being denied entry to Brazil en masse.

In late July, the Russian Telegram channel Baza reported that 10 pregnant women had been "deported" from Russia. The information was later picked up by various media outlets. However, the Brazilian police denied the veracity of the report to DW, explaining that decisions to deny somebody entry to the country were always made on a case-by-case basis, and that pregnancy played no role in the process.

DW was only able to find one documented case of a pregnant Russian woman being initially refused entry into Brazil. She was allowed to enter the country after a lawyer intervened. According to the court records, the Brazilian border authorities had doubts as to how the Russian national would be financing her stay in Brazil.

The woman did not respond to the DW's inquiries.

This article was originally written in Russian.

card_5.headline: Trump hails 'major progress' in setting up US base in Poland
card_5.article_content:
US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that significant progress had been made toward establishing a US military base in Poland.

"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

In August, Warsaw revealed that it was in talks with Washington regarding a permanent US military presence in Poland.

"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance," Trump added in a social media post.

His announcement comes despite his administration's launch of a formal review of its military presence in Europe. This has raised fears among allies that the US could reduce its military presence there.

Nawrocki, who is a conservative ally of the US president, thanked Trump on X, saying  Poland was "ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation."

He added, "I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base."

Meanwhile, Zbigniew Bogucki, the head of the Polish president's chancellery, called Trump's announcement "great news for Poland." He also noted that it came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland.

In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said his country was discussing with the United States the possibility of establishing a permanent US base on its territory.

"We have already completed the initial stage of the process, not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told the public broadcaster TVP.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been pushing for a larger allied presence on NATO's eastern flank.

Nearly 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland, a member of both NATO and the EU. However, they are there almost exclusively on a rotational basis.

Poland's proximity to Ukraine and Russia is a key factor in its security strategy. The country allocates approximately 5% of its gross domestic product to defense spending and has been working to increase the United States' military presence.

card_6.headline: US: Trump administration weakens Endangered Species Act
card_6.article_content:
The US government is planning a major reinterpretation of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), The New York Times reported and officials confirmed to AFP on Thursday.

The policy shift was delivered in a new memo signed by Brian Nesvik, director of the Interior Department's Fish and Wildlife Service.

In it, the department will reduce the term "take," a term that relates to pursuing, killing or capturing of a species, to simply "affirmative conduct intentionally directed against a particular animal or animals."

This change would no longer treat the unintentional killing of protected wildlife as unlawful.

Wildlife deaths resulting from foreseeable risks posed by activities such as commercial fishing or logging would end up exempt from the landmark 1973 law.

The wildlife service has historically held people liable for accidentally harming protected species such as grizzly bears, manatees and spotted owls.

"This cuts against the entire history of the Endangered Species Act," Dan Ashe, who led the Fish and Wildlife Service under former President Barack Obama, told the Associated Press. "It just creates a huge loophole. It completely relieves people of any responsibility for their actions, even consequences that can be easily predicted."

The Interior Department confirmed the memo's authenticity to AFP.

"The memorandum accurately reflects the US Fish and Wildlife Service's guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm,'" the department told AFP.

"Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," it added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Last year, the Trump administration declared it would consider "economic considerations" when deciding whether to protect species at risk of extinction.

The move is the latest attempt to loosen the landmark ESA's rules. Combined, the changes overturn five decades of precedent in how the law is interpreted and applied.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has argued that the changes are necessary, claiming the ESA has been "weaponized" to stop economic projects, weaken competitiveness, undermine national security, and ultimately hurt Americans.

Among the changes to ESA is the redefinition of the term "harm," which would allow oil drilling, mining and other activities in endangered habitats as long as those activities do not directly kill or injure the animals.

The automatic application of endangered species protections to those listed as "threatened" was also halted.

Additionally, the Trump administration announced that it was shrinking two vast stretches of protected land in Utah by more than 90%, to open millions of acres of protected land for fossil fuel extraction and mining.

Last week, the attorneys general of 20 Democratic-led states, along with Washington, DC, submitted a lawsuit against the administration over its overhaul of ESA.

One lawsuit tackles the redefinition of "harm," while a second lawsuit challenges a rule that removes protections for newly threatened species, and the new business-related considerations taken into account when declaring "critical habitats."

"The Trump administration is trying to undermine the law, the will of Congress and the will of the people ‌who overwhelmingly support protections for endangered species," Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said.

"Instead of stewardship, this administration's approach to our land, to ‌our water is one of exploitation," he added.

card_1.headline: Frank Stronach will not face jail time for indecent assault conviction, judge says
card_1.article_content:
WARNING: This story refers to sexual assault allegations and may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

Canadian billionaire Frank Stronach will not serve any time in jail for his conviction of indecent assault, an Ontario judge said on Thursday.

Ontario Crown prosecutors had been asking that the 94-year-old founder of auto-parts giant Magna International be sentenced to six months in jail for that conviction.

But at the end of the sentencing hearing on Thursday, Ontario Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy said while she hadn't yet decided the sentence she would impose, jail time would not be part of her decision.

Molloy said she had "very firmly" decided that, based on the circumstances of the case, she would not be sentencing someone who is 94 to a jail term. Court will return on Dec. 11 for that decision.

Assistant Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic had also asked for a Sex Offender Information Registration Act (SOIRA) order and that Stronach be placed on Canada’s National Sex Offender Registry for 10 years.

Molloy asked Vlacic what she would consider to be a reasonable conditional sentence for Stronach. Vlacic said six months house arrest with exceptions for medical appointments and court appearances.

When his judge-alone trial began in a Toronto courtroom in February, Stronach was facing 12 charges related to allegations of sexual assault from seven women dating back almost 50 years.

But at his sentencing hearing on Thursday, the 94-year-old founder of auto-parts giant Magna International is facing sentencing on just one of those charges — indecent assault.

On that charge, one of the women had told the court that Stronach invited her to a midtown Toronto apartment sometime in the fall of 1977, and while there, he bent her over the arm of a chair, lifted up her skirt and tried to rape her.

In a victim impact statement on Thursday, the woman told court that she had felt ambushed and overpowered by Stronach and that her physical privacy had been violated without her consent.

The woman, whose identity is protected by a court-ordered publication ban, said the assault had destroyed her sense of safety in social settings and that her feeling of apprehension is ongoing.

"I felt that I deserved an apology. I was upset when none was forthcoming," she told the court.

"The impact of an assault is not limited to the physical. It can also jolt one's identity and personality," she said. "Recovering one's comfort with people requires time and resilience, and it may never be complete."

Vlacic, the Crown prosecutor, argued that the passage of time since the assault occurred is a consideration but that people need to be held to account for their conduct.

She said those found guilty must pay for their crimes and that to do otherwise would encourage people to lie low and bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

But Stronach's lawyer, Leora Shemesh, countered that her client, instead of any jail time, should receive an absolute discharge — meaning the finding of guilty would remain but no conviction would be registered and Stronach would not have a criminal record. The finding of guilt would still come up in a background check but only for a year.

She also argued that Stronach should not be registered as a sex offender.
