Shemesh went through a list of Stronach's accomplishments and contributions to society, stressing as well that until these charges, he had had no brushes with the law.

She told the court that Stronach faces only one charge from the initial 12 and that this particular offence of indecent assault, "on the continuum of sexual or indecent assault, is on the least serious end of the spectrum."

"The Crown's position is manifestly excessive, ... unreasonable and seems quite un-Canadian," Shemesh said, noting how Stronach's honours have been revoked, his name has been stripped from various centres and "dragged through the mud," and he has suffered and been punished enough.

Stronach had been charged with attempted rape and indecent assault for that particular incident. But during the course of the trial, the Crown dropped the attempted rape charge.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy presided over Stronach's judge-alone trial. (Alexandra Newbould/CBC)

In her decision, Molloy agreed that much of what the witness described had happened, but also agreed with the Crown's decision to withdraw the attempted rape charge because it was unclear whether Stronach would have been able to penetrate the woman based on her state of dress at the time.

Still, Molloy referred to it as "gross and disgusting conduct," which is why she found him guilty of indecent assault. The offence is a historical charge, having been repealed from the Criminal Code in 1983. That means anyone charged similarly today would face a sexual assault charge.

In June, Molloy also found Stronach guilty of sexual assault related to another woman who said Stronach groped her in his Toronto Harbourfront condo sometime in 1983 or 1984. The woman said she had gone to meet him for dinner to discuss why she had been fired as a waitress at his then restaurant, Rooney's. She said Stronach invited her to his condo, which is where he groped her.

Molloy said she was "completely convinced" by the woman's evidence. Molloy did, however, "with considerable trepidation," describe it as a minor sexual assault, saying that the conduct was at the "low end" of the spectrum of sexual assault.

However, weeks after the decision, emails were presented in court from the woman's lawyer in a separate civil complaint. Stronach's lawyer Leora Shemesh alleged those emails told a story inconsistent with the woman's testimony in the criminal trial.

Molloy then granted a mistrial on the sexual assault conviction. The Crown is appealing that decision.

Throughout the trial, which lasted more than two months, the Crown withdrew a number of charges following the testimony and cross-examination of some of the complainants, saying there was not sufficient evidence to sustain findings of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on those particular counts.

By the time Molloy was set to render her decision in June, Stronach was facing five counts related to three women.

Crown appealing post-verdict mistrial in Frank Stronach sexual assault conviction

Canadian businessman Frank Stronach found guilty of sexual assault, indecent assault

All of the initial seven complainants, whose allegations span the period between 1977 and 1990, testified in court, offering an emotional account of the sexual offences they say they experienced at the hands of Stronach.

Stronach, who was in court every day but never took the witness box in his own defence, had denied the allegations and pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Meanwhile, Stronach is set to face another trial in Newmarket, Ont., next year. When Stronach was initially arrested in June 2024, he was charged with 18 offences involving 13 complainants. But the case was split into two trials later that year.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

card_3.headline: Judge denies Tamara Lich's request to take Caribbean cruise and visit the White House under house arrest
card_3.article_content:
A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to the White House.

Lich was found guilty in April 2025 of mischief and other offences for her role in organizing and sustaining the 2022 convoy protest that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for nearly a month.

She was handed a conditional sentence last October that included 12 months under house arrest.

A month after being sentenced, Lich asked for and received permission to leave her home in Medicine Hat, Alta., to attend her grandchildren's school. Since then, she has travelled to other provinces for her job with Rebel News.

In July, Lich asked for permission to travel internationally.

Lich appeared virtually in court from the passenger seat of a vehicle on Thursday, wearing a Rebel News hoodie as the ruling was read.

"The fact that an activity can be described as work does not compel permission to leave the jurisdiction," said Justice Heather Perkins-McVey, spending around 45 minutes sharing her reasons for the decision.

Lich was also told there must be "legitimate circumstances" for temporary travel outside of Alberta. Perkins-McVey instructed Lich to make individual requests to do so.

In her initial request to travel abroad, Lich didn't offer the court a detailed itinerary, but her request mentioned attending press events at the White House, going on a seven-day Caribbean cruise with Rebel News, and travelling to Arizona to speak with Rob Schneider, a right-wing comedian whose controversial content prompted his removal from a Saskatchewan stage in 2024.

Crown prosecutors said the additional exemptions would give her a "blank cheque" to travel internationally. They opposed the request, arguing that granting it was unnecessary and would diminish the impact of her sentence "to an unacceptable extent."

Her defence said in July she had "abided by the terms of her conditional sentence to the letter."

In Perkins-McVey's ruling Thursday, she said there was not enough evidence to show Lich's request is needed, including to maintain employment, and it would go against the principle of her sentence.

The judge characterized the Rebel-sponsored Caribbean cruise as a "commercial event" and "fundraiser." She said the Arizona trip was "promotional" and much of the proposed international work could be completed from Canada.

Speaking after court, Lich's lawyer Lawrence Greenspon said the judge's decision was "very considered"

"There's nothing in what the judge said today, or in the sentence itself, that prevents (Lich) in any way from speaking freely, and associating freely and working to the extent that she can by the conditions that were imposed."

Fellow 2022 convoy leader Chris Barber, who was convicted and sentenced alongside Lich, travels south of the border through his work as a commercial truck driver.

Sentenced Oct. 7, 2025, the two have already served the bulk of their sentences; but they are far from being done with Ontario courtrooms.

Crown prosecutors are appealing the judge's findings and sentencing, arguing both should have been found guilty of more crimes than they were as well as given harsher sentences. Barber and Lich have accepted their sentences, but are appealing the judge's initial decision.

The Ontario Court of Appeal isn't likely to hear those arguements until early 2027.

Lich and Barber are also involved in civil court matters.

Buffalo Bills to 'celebrate' O Canada at home opener amid more Trump threats during trade war

"The further they can expand their footprint, going into southern Ontario, going into Toronto... that really matters to the Buffalo Bills. They're a team that wants to make sure they have all their bases covered for people to be welcomed in."

On Wednesday, the team posted a video on social media platform X showing retired Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick and retired wide receiver Stevie Johnson complete a few cross-border catches along the Niagara River, tossing to each other from aboard distant ferries.

Niagara Parks, the Ontario agency that manages the Canadian side of the Niagara River, said in a news release on Wednesday that the successful boat to boat passes "will be aired during NFL on Prime’s broadcast of the Buffalo Bills first 2026 home game on Thursday, September 17."

Former Buffalo Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick, now retired, played a game of catch across the border with former Bills wide receiver Stevie Johnson on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, a day before the team plays its first home game of the 2026 season. (Niagara Parks)

Actress and singer Auliʻi Cravalho will perform the American anthem and Toronto band Barenaked Ladies will sing O Canada.

In April, fans at KeyBank Center in Buffalo sang O Canada after a microphone failed before the Sabres' playoff game against the Boston Bruins.

Canadian rock band Barenaked Ladies will sing O'Canada before the Buffalo Bills season opener on Thursday Sept. 17, 2026. (Matt Barnes)

card_5.headline: Far-right German politician heckles Carney with 'U.S.A.' chant before EU address
card_5.article_content:
As Prime Minister Mark Carney approached the podium at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, he was met by a lone heckler with an unexpected chant for a Canadian leader speaking to the EU in France.

"U.S.A.! U.S.A.!" German MEP Siegbert Droese called out.

Some in the crowd groaned, then Carney chuckled and carried on with his speech where he called for closer ties between Canada and the EU and an "alliance for the future."

In a statement provided to CBC News, Droese said the chant was his way of "addressing the geopolitical elephant in the room."

‘U.S.A., U.S.A.': German politician chants as Carney speaks to EU Parliament

Droese said Carney's reaction to his callout shows the prime minister "clearly has a sense of humor."

Carney's address to the Parliament in Strasbourg is just another step in a bilateral push for a tightened relationship with the EU and comes just a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the bloc's first "associate member" — a new, and as of yet, undefined title.

Read Mark Carney's full speech to the European Parliament

What we know about the proposed partnership between Canada and the EU

"It was an absurd and unrealistic knee-jerk reaction for Ms. von der Leyen to propose an 'associate EU membership' for Canada: a status not provided for in any of the European treaties," Droese wrote in his statement.

Droese is a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been surging in popularity among German voters.

A 'Make America Great Again' hat sits on the desk of the German Member of European Parliament Siegbert Frank Droese in 2024. (Virginia Mayo/The Associated Press)

The AfD's domestic policies include proposing large-scale deportations of anyone of non-German heritage and a push for what the party calls a patriotic cultural policy to cut funding for projects not deemed suitably national — such as some Holocaust remembrance programs.

In his statement, Droese called the European Commission president corrupt and suggested she's seeking an agreement with Canada to bypass her "abysmal" relations with the U.S.

Droese ended his statement by saying there is a "certain irony in the fact that the six letters 'USA! USA!' were enough" to trigger a reaction.

card_10.headline: More than 500,000 Albertans have applied to vote by mail in referendum: Elections Alberta
card_10.article_content:
More than half a million Albertans have applied to vote by mail in the upcoming referendum, according to Elections Alberta.

An agency spokesperson told CBC News Thursday it has received more than 509,000 requests for special ballots, with eight days left for electors to apply for that voting method.

Elections Alberta has known for weeks that there was greater demand to vote by mail in the referendum scheduled for Oct. 19. But the number of requests received so far is already more than eight times greater than the roughly 60,000 special ballots requested in the 2023 provincial election.

The Oct. 19 referendum features 10 questions on a variety of issues. Most notably, the list includes a question about whether Alberta should remain in Canada or whether the provincial government should start the process to hold a binding referendum on secession.

Special mail-in ballot requests surge above 175,000 ahead of Alberta referendum

Elections Alberta also says it's working with jails and prisons to ensure inmates can vote. Incarcerated Albertans vote through mail-in ballots.

The agency couldn't say how many inmates have requested ballots for the referendum, but it said just over 400 applied to vote in the 2023 election.

The Correctional Service of Canada says staff have been ensuring inmates are aware of their right to vote and that posters about the upcoming referendum have been put up throughout institutions in Alberta.

There are almost three million eligible voters in the province, according to Elections Alberta, meaning about 17 per cent have expressed intentions to vote by mail in this election.

The last provincial referendum, in 2021, saw voter turnout of about 39 per cent.

Elections Alberta is also making headway toward having the number of people it needs for referendum day.

The agency set out to recruit 60,000 electoral workers. It has launched a recruitment campaign and even solicited electoral management bodies in other parts of Canada to help out.

Elections Alberta soliciting help from other jurisdictions to carry out fall referendum

A spokesperson said that, as of Thursday, almost 48,000 people have applied to be election officers. They didn't have a total number of how many were hired.

Elections Alberta, however, is still working to ensure each electoral division has enough staff. The spokesperson said it needs more applications in the following constituencies:

Elections Alberta will keep looking for election officers until voting starts on referendum day, its spokesperson said.

card_11.headline: UN mission finds 'grounds to believe' U.S. committed war crimes in strikes on Iranian school, sports centre
card_11.article_content:
A United Nations fact-finding mission on Iran said Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school ‌and sports facility in Iran in February and that these constituted war crimes.

It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests that occurred just weeks before the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes in Iran on Feb. 28.

The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the American conduct during the Iran war and ​the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.

Video appears to contradict Trump claim that U.S. wasn't responsible for deadly Minab school blast

The Iranian and U.S. ​permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to requests by Reuters for comment.

U.S. officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.

The White House issued a scathing statement in response to the report.

"The UN Human Rights Council has accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades," said White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly.

"The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbours in the region."

The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the UN's top human rights body, which is based in Geneva.

The experts were expected to present their findings on Monday to the council, which is made up of 47 UN member countries.

The ​UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh ⁠Primary School in Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according ‌to Iranian officials.

The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.

WATCH | Internal investigation reportedly finds U.S. responsible for strike on Iran school:

U.S. responsible for strike on Iran school, internal military probe reportedly finds

According to the report, the U.S. failure to update information in relation to the school in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence. The school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex.

"Rather, the U.S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."

Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report

Reuters first reported that an initial internal U.S. military investigation showed American forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab. The Pentagon has since elevated the probe, but it has not published any preliminary findings. U.S. President Donald Trump initially blamed Iran for the attack.

UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found ​no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.

A picture of Elham Zaeri, one of the victims of a strike on a sports hall on Feb. 28, is shown in Lamerd, Iran. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)

The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd, Iran. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and ⁠a school, and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.

U.S. Central Command said in ⁠a statement in March that American forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.

The UN mission ⁠probe found ⁠that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic ​attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.

Rights groups ​say bystanders were among those killed ⁠during the biggest crackdown since Shia Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes, including the U.S. and Israel.

Reporting from inside Iran

The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people were injured.

The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of ⁠the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from ‌previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

card_13.headline: NASA satellite discovers a new crater on the moon that's bigger than the Colosseum
card_13.article_content:
Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.

The steep-sided hole — 222 metres across and up to 43 metres deep — is the solar system's biggest known impact crater carved out in recent times.

Such a large-scale event is estimated to occur only once every 132 years, researchers said, making this a treasure trove of information as NASA prepares to build a base for astronauts on the moon.

"This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation," the scientists wrote in one of two studies appearing on the subject Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) spotted the crater on the moon's near side in May 2024 soon after it was formed by an incoming fragment of an asteroid or comet. The moon strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space.

A zoomed-in view of McGetchin Crater, circled on the left, next to a 'before' image on the right. (NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

LRO's wide-angle images were not identified in the crush of data until August 2025. The spacecraft gathered more detailed pictures last fall, followed by confirmation of the discovery early this year.

The crater is named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston's Lunar and Planetary Institute.

Pockmarked since ancient times, the moon bears some of the solar system's largest impact craters, including one that stretches more than 2,400 kilometres across.

This latest impact churned the lunar surface for more than 100 kilometres. Dust and rocky soil were hurled away at a higher angle than expected, according to Mark Robinson, chief scientist for the LRO's cameras who works at Intuitive Machines. Robinson was the lead author for one of the studies.

Here's the mark a SpaceX rocket crash left on the moon

Astronauts' movement increased subsurface temperatures on the moon, study finds

A separate study identified a seven-kilometre-wide cold spot around the new crater, consistent with a loosening of the moon's topsoil. Co-author David Paige of the University of California, Los Angeles, likens it to gardening.

"We're now thinking of impacts as a way to garden the regolith — churning the sediments and putting stuff above that's usually below the surface," Paige said in a statement. (Regolith is the term for the loose, solid material on top of bedrock.)

An overhead, close-up view of McGetchin Crater that was taken on Dec. 5, 2025, by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. (NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

The LRO's numerous crater discoveries since its launch in 2009 show that the moon's top two centimetres of soil is being overturned by ejected material every 80,000 years, faster than previously thought, according to Robinson.

Contrary to the popular belief that the Apollo moonwalkers' dusty lunar footprints will last forever, they will "definitely be long gone in that time frame," Robinson said in an email.

The next step is to calculate the risk of ejected crater material striking NASA's planned moon base, he added.

"That information will help engineers harden structures so one won't have to worry about damage, or maybe worry less."

card_14.headline: Alasko frozen raspberries recalled in 7 provinces over norovirus risk
card_14.author: Bobbi-Jean MacKinnon
card_14.article_content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency is warning about a recall on certain Alasko brand frozen, whole raspberries sold in seven provinces, due to possible norovirus contamination.

Norovirus is a very contagious virus that causes diarrhea and vomiting.

The recall was triggered after an investigation by the agency into a foodborne illness outbreak, according to the advisory, issued this week.

"There have been reported illnesses associated with the consumption of these products," it says.

No information about the location of the outbreak or how many people are sick is provided.

The affected products include:

Both products have best before dates of Nov. 10, 2027, the code PO#138602, and LOT# SY25314.

They were sold to the general public as well as hotels, restaurants and institutions in the following provinces:

The recalled products were sold to the general public as well as hotels, restaurants and institutions, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency said. (Canadian Food Inspection Agency)

"Do not consume, serve, use, sell, or distribute recalled products," the advisory says.

Recalled products should be thrown out or returned to the location where they were purchased.

The agency said it continues to investigate, which may lead to the recall of other products.

It's also verifying that industry is removing the recalled products from the marketplace.

People who think they became sick from consuming a recalled product should contact their health-care provider, the agency said.

Norovirus symptoms may start as soon as 12 hours after exposure, according to the Public Health Agency of Canada's website.

In addition to diarrhea, vomiting, the main symptoms are nausea and stomach pain and cramps, it says.

Other symptoms may include low-grade fever, headache, chills, muscle aches and fatigue.

Recalled products should be thrown out or returned to the location where they were purchased, the CFIA advised. (Canadian Food Inspection Agency)

There is no prescription medication to treat norovirus infections, but most people feel better within two to three days, with no long-term health effects.

Diarrhea or vomiting can cause dehydration, however. The Public Health Agency of Canada recommends people with norovirus drink plenty of liquids to replace lost body fluids. People with a severe case may need to be hospitalized and given fluids through a needle, it notes.

People can become infected with norovirus more than once.
